newsitem.title: LEBANON: FEATURE - U.S. to decide if Americans are safe in Lebanon.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - U.S. to decide if Americans are safe in Lebanon.

text.p: The U.S. ambassador's bullet-proof convoy races by in a scene reminiscent of Lebanon's bloody 1980s when 241 U.S. servicemen were killed in a suicide bombing and Americans were kidnapped and murdered.
Sirens wail above vehicles mounted with machineguns. Security guards with high-tech goggles scan the streets for potential gunmen. Traffic is ordered to stop.
The Lebanese, eager to show they have permanently abandoned the guns, rockets and bombs of the 1975-90 civil war, describe these security measures as absurd.

For policy-makers thousands of miles away in Washington, the security precautions are a reminder that the United States suffered its most humiliating Middle East experience in this vibrant city that is now hungry for foreign investment.
On July 31 Washington is to make a decision that could improve Lebanon's tarnished image or further frustrate a country once known as the Switzerland of the Middle East.
It will once again debate whether to end a ban on its citizens entering Lebanon, imposed in 1985 after Moslem zealots hijacked a TWA airliner to Beirut and killed a U.S. passenger.
The outcome is seen as a barometer of international confidence in Beirut, labelled the world's most dangerous city for foreigners in the late 1980s because of kidnappings by Moslem fundamentalists.
POLITICAL PRESSURE OR SAFETY ISSUE?
Officials and ordinary Lebanese see the ban, which was not followed by other countries, as U.S. pressure on Lebanon in the currently moribund peace talks with Israel.
Lifting it would be a boost for billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri, the entrepreneur leading Lebanon's multi-billion dollar reconstruction drive.
"Lebanon is safe for Americans. It is safer than many other countries where Americans live and work," Hariri told Reuters.
Continuing the ban would send the Lebanese government back to the drawing board in efforts to prove that this is a safe place for Western tourists, and more importantly, businessmen.
The U.S. State Department ban on travel says "the situation in Lebanon is so dangerous that no U.S. citizen can be considered safe from terrorist acts."

According to unofficial U.S. estimates more than 20,000 American citizens live here and between 40,000 and 50,000, most of whom also have Lebanese citizenship, travel to Beirut each year. An embassy official conceded she did not know of any direct threat against Americans in recent years.
AMERICANS HAUNTED BY BLOODY BEIRUT MEMORIES
The U.S. National Security Adviser Sandy Berger said last month that Secretary of State Madeleine Albright was taking a fresh look at the travel ban.

But it will not be easy for the Clinton administration to lower its guard or bury memories of the 1980s. The Americans lost 241 servicemen in a 1983 suicide truck bombing at the marines base at Beirut airport. Dozens of other U.S. citizens died in two suicide bomb attacks on embassy buildings.
There are still Lebanese hardliners who make the U.S. government nervous.

Sitting in his Beirut office where armed bodyguards frisk visitors and take their mobile telephones for fear of hidden bombs, former Hizbollah leader Sheikh Sobhi Tufaili talked earlier this year of his plans for Americans.
"We will shoot them," said the radical Shi'ite cleric, who condemns the pro-Iranian Hizbollah (Party of God) as too soft but still has a following in the group.

A few weeks later, before several thousand supporters in the Bekaa Valley, where some of the world's most dreaded guerrilla groups have had bases, he called on the Lebanese government to expel the United States ambassador.
"We will kill the Israelis. But first, we will kill the Americans," he said.
LEBANESE AND AMERICAN RESIDENTS SAY IT IS SAFE
But the Beirut government and average Lebanese interviewed dismiss the fears of U.S. officials who say Hizbollah and other guerrilla groups remain active.

"Don't you think it's safer here than in America?" asked Ziyad, a Lebanese-American who manages Beirut's thriving Hard Rock Cafe, where customers listen to American rock in a restaurant lined with musical memorabilia.
"Here I can go to the cash machine at the bank at three in the morning. I can't do that in the United States and feel safe."
Americans in Lebanon told Reuters they feel safe.
"The travel ban is ridiculous," said a woman who worked for an American who was kidnapped in the 1980s.
"His kidnapping brought things closer to home. But now I feel safe. The tide changes here very quickly. But I feel safe," added the woman, whose blonde hair makes her stand out in a crowd.
Another American, Lauri Irani, said she even feels safe walking in the Shi'ite southern suburbs of Beirut, a Hizbollah stronghold.
"People here invite you into their shops. People are against U.S. policies but individuals are safe," she said from a cellular phone on the beach.
The easy lifestyle of many Americans is a world away from the U.S. diplomats at the fortress-like embassy on an isolated hillside outside Beirut.
Guards in camouflage and clutching automatic rifles stand near a watchtower with a heavy machinegun overlooking the road to the compound which is surrounded with barbed wire.
